https://www.dw.com/en/india-cockroach-mo.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5J5Yp The CJP says it will ask local citizens to document issues with government schools in India [FILE: September 2018] Image: Prabhat Kumar Verma/ZUMA/picture alliance Advertisement The student protest movement in India known as the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) scored a major victory in July after Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan stepped down following weeks of demonstrations in Delhi. Now, the movement is aiming its campaign for accountability at improving India's government schools. Last week on India's Independence Day, the CJP launched a nationwide campaign asking citizens to inspect government schools, document what is missing and pressure local authorities to fix basic facilities. Dubbed "Fix the Schools," the campaign aims to mobilize citizens to identify problems locally and make them public. CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke launched a campaign in the Indian state of Maharashtra from his native village in Hingoli district. He spoke with students and documented what he said were broken windows, lack of clean drinking water, missing classroom benches and unusable bathrooms. "No matter which political party ruled, nobody worked for government schools in states. Now there is a need, and we can make them work by asking questions," said Dipke. Government officials did not respond to DW's requests for comment on the CJP's accusations. What does the plan call for? The CJP has prepared assessment forms that parents, students and residents can use to document issues with local government schools. They are being asked to record video evidence, complete the assessment and send the material to CJP. The CJP launched its campaign in the state of Maharashtra, where these children attend a one-room school in Khaparmal village Image: Shefali Rafiq/AFP The organization plans to compile the reports into a public record of neglected schools and use them to pressure local authorities to respond. The CJP has said the campaign will focus on five basic requirements: functioning toilets, electricity, clean drinking water, classroom benches and the quality of midday meals. One element is to publicly recognize village heads who improve their local schools. The CJP plans to use before-and-after evidence to highlight villages where conditions have improved. The organization has set an initial target of auditing at least 100 rural government schools over the next two months and pressing authorities to act on the findings. CJP seeks to expand support The youth-led CJP began in May as a campaign calling for accountability over a scandal involving a highly competitive university entrance exam. The news that the question sheet had been leaked ahead of the exam date in early May exposed long-running grievances over privileged access for some students. Fueled by millions of young followers on social media, the movement soon tapped into wider frustrations over unemployment, shrinking opportunities and an education system many young Indians believe has failed them. After the education minister stepped down, and the government promised steps toward accountability for those involved in the exam paper leaks, the CJP has shifted focus. However, to be effective in localities around India, the youth-based movement, which has initially mainly been based in Delhi, will need to broaden its appeal . This comes as Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, in his Independence Day address, placed youth power at the center of his vision for a developed India. India's youth a political force Aruna Roy, a prominent Indian social activist and former civil servant who helped lead a grassroots movement that resulted in India's landmark Right to Information Act in 2005, said the CJP's campaign could tap into a wider constituency of young people seeking greater accountability . "The demands at Jantar Mantar resonated with young people across the country," Roy said, referring to the location in central Delhi where the protests were based. "It was, in many cases, a spontaneous revolt against the state for failing to deliver on promises affecting their education, employment and future," Roy told DW. "When young people have decided to fight against the destruction of their dreams, they are formidable," she added. CJP opens door for 'citizen audits' Responsibility for government school infrastructure is spread across state governments, local administrations and elected village bodies, while conditions vary widely across India. The CJP's new campaign is a test of whether the movement's ability to mobilize students, volunteers, money and public attention outside traditional political structures can be sustained beyond last month's high-profile victory . Amrita Johri, an activist and transparency advocate, said CJP had tapped into larger issues with India's education system. "Millions of young people have lost precious years and resources because of repeated failures to ensure fair examinations, with little accountability for those responsible," Johri told DW. "Every government school should publicly disclose its spending, infrastructure, teacher vacancies and midday meal provision," Johri said. "The CJP can make this meaningful by training volunteers to systematically document problems and follow up, while helping local communities use tools such as the Right to Information to demand change," she added. Social activist Roy said citizen audits could turn public anger into sustained pressure for accountability. "Citizen audits are vital because they expose corruption and the arbitrary use of power and bring people into the struggle for accountability," she said. The campaign gives parents and residents a direct role in documenting what they see around them. CJP has said they do not need to wait for an official inspection to identify a broken toilet, a school without drinking water or classrooms without basic furniture. India's Cockroach movement — and why it matters To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What comes next? The first test will be whether its target of 100 schools produces visible changes, and whether the model can be replicated beyond the places where CJP already has organizers and supporters. The organization has also indicated that it could extend the citizen audit model to public healthcare facilities, widening its focus from education to other basic government services. N. Sai Balaji, former president of the All India Students' Association, said CJP was broadening the fight over education reform and creating the possibility of convergence with student movements already campaigning on higher education. "The two will meet, and there is a clear synergy. The impact will be felt as the momentum builds," Balaji told DW. For a movement that began with a protest over examination irregularities, the next phase is less about taking to the streets and more about documenting what citizens encounter in their everyday lives. "We have built a new parliament, a new PM house. Why have we not been able to build new schools in our villages? Do we not consider the children of farmers and laborers the future of our country?" asked CJP leader Dipke in a video message. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Polish defence spending as a share of GDP has more than doubled from 2.2% to 4.8% this year. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Polish defence spending as a share of GDP has more than doubled from 2.2% to 4.8% this year. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images Poland Poland is racing ahead with military spending – but will it help or damage its economic growth story? In the first article in a series on the Polish economy, we look at the country’s defence boom and its implications Richard Partington in Warsaw Sun 27 Sep 2026 01.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 06.08 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A short distance north from Warsaw along the Vistula river, camouflaged missile launchers roll through the quiet village of Czosnów. As recently as two years ago, their destination – a hi-tech weapons facility opened this month – had been a cornfield. Now, as Poland drives up defence investment at one of the fastest rates in the developed world, this rural spot has been transformed amid Europe’s response to Russian aggression and US disengagement. “Everyone has had to move twice as fast to meet the Polish needs,” says Jim Price, the managing director of MBDA Polska, the local subsidiary of the European multinational arms group. Based in the UK, the former Royal Marine says Poland is shifting from importing its weapons to manufacturing them at home. “When it became clear there is a need to defend Nato’s eastern flank, in the event of a war itself, they needed to be able to do things in the blink of an eye. So we decided to invest in-the country to create a facility. We had to build up our Polish subsidiary – and that means Polish jobs.” Poland’s defence budget has grown at a blistering pace. Since Vladimir Putin ordered Russian troops into Ukraine almost five years ago, spending as a share of Polish gross domestic product (GDP ) has more than doubled from 2.2% to 4.8% this year. In cash terms, this equates to $53bn (£39.8bn), the fourth-highest in the EU after Germany, France and Italy. graph showing Poland’s defence spending Attention in Warsaw is clearly focused on the risk of an imminent Russian test of Nato resolve. However, there is also another motive: growing the economy. Inside the soundproofed, airlock-style doors enclosing his office in Warsaw, Marcin Bosacki, Poland’s deputy foreign minister, says Russian aggression is heavily influencing the Polish government’s plans for economic development and cooperation with EU and Nato allies. “[It] is clearly benefiting Polish security; Polish defence, and the Polish economy as well,” he says. Strengthening economic ties in the pursuit of military readiness would discourage Putin (“a traditional Russian imperialist”) from attacking Nato, Bosacki adds. View image in fullscreen Marcin Bosacki says strengthening economic ties in the pursuit of military readiness would discourage Moscow from attacking Nato. Photograph: Anna Liminowicz/The Guardian “The only thing which Putin understands is solidarity and power. And so the more we are united and strong, the less likely the outcome of more aggressive Russian provocations against Nato member states is.” Hope remains for a diplomatic solution. This month, Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held talks in Moscow with Putin and in Kyiv with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Next month, further negotiations are scheduled in Abu Dhabi. However, diplomatic sources believe Russia is unlikely to cede ground – rendering Nato’s demonstrations of military readiness critical. History shows defence and economics are closely intertwined. Statisticians first devised GDP as a metric in response to the 1930s Great Depression and needs of wartime planning to gauge the capacity of an economy. View image in fullscreen The Gdańsk shipyard, the birthplace of Poland’s Solidarity movement. Photograph: Anna Liminowicz/The Guardian Poland has been through an economic miracle since the Solidarność (solidarity) movement that arose from the Gdańsk shipyard strikes paved the way for its transition from communism almost four decades ago. Living standards have shot up from 40% of the EU average in the mid-1990s to 81% last year. Joining the EU in 2004 and securing catch-up funds from Brussels – which was spent on new roads, railways, and other productivity-enhancing infrastructure – also helped. Annual output surpassed $1tn (£755bn) last year, with Poland among the fastest-growing EU countries at an annualised rate of 3.9% in the second quarter despite the global headwinds caused by the Iran war . Graph showing increase in Poland’s GDP per capita relative to EU average between 1996 and 2025 However, Poland’s defence boom is not cost-free. Nor has economic development helped it avoid political polarisation. The rising military budget is among the reasons why Poland is predicted to run the biggest fiscal deficit in the EU next year, at 7.1% of GDP. Last week, Moody’s downgraded the country’s long-term sovereign credit rating to the lowest level since 2002, amid an apparent lack of willingness to rebuild fiscal buffers. Leszek Kąsek, a Warsaw-based economist at ING Bank, said: “This path is not sustainable. You should ask people if Poland can maintain its growth story and whether politicians will be ready to adjust?” View image in fullscreen Wedged between larger neighbours it has been subjugated twice within living memory, Poles are uneasy about national security. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images Wedged between larger neighbours it has been subjugated twice within living memory, Poles are uneasy about national security. But despite its economic turnaround under EU membership, and as it secures billions of euros in defence funds from Brussels, support for Eurosceptic politics remains. In the run-up to the general election next year, the defence of the country, support for Ukraine and EU relations will be highly politically charged. Outside the foreign ministry in Warsaw, protesters wave placards in a “Poles for peace” nationalist rally, organised by rightwing politicians opposed to the EU and its support for Ukraine. Inside the building’s marble halls, where the Polish flag appears to be positioned next to those of Nato and the EU at almost every opportunity, Bosacki says divisions over the benefits to Poland of membership to both institutions has emerged for the first time. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion graph showing Countries on Nato’s eastern flank spend a larger share of their This year, Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, who has backing from the rightwing Law and Justice party, attempted to block the Polish prime minister Donald Tusk’s liberal, pro-EU government from accessing €44bn (£38bn) of defence investment loans approved under the bloc’s security action for Europe (Safe) programme. “I think our right is so eager to regain power they will use anything,” Bosacki says. “Here for the first time, the opposition was [against doing] something which, in my opinion – and the opinion of the majority of Poles – is clearly benefiting Polish security, Polish defence and the Polish economy as well.” Through Safe, Warsaw secured the largest single disbursement in the loan programme. The government has pledged to channel almost 90% of it to domestic industry – led by Polska Grupa Zbrojeniowa (PGZ), the state-owned defence conglomerate. However, in the race to build up capacity, the tills are ringing for US-arms manufacturers supplying Patriot missiles, Abrams tanks and F-35 fighter jets. In March, the International Monetary Fund cautioned that the positive economic spillovers from EU defence investment would not necessarily flow for the governments taking out their chequebooks. However, Warsaw is doing defence deals with international partners, including the UK, to help develop its domestic manufacturing base at the same time as building military readiness. View image in fullscreen Yvette Cooper, then the UK foreign secretary, visits the Miecznik (swordfish) programme at the PGZ naval shipyard in Gdynia in June. Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PA The British defence group Babcock is working with PGZ to help build a fleet of new frigates. Known as the Miecznik, or swordfish, programme, the company has a shipyard at Gdynia on the Baltic coast. The first ship was launched this summer by Tusk. “It’s a must for Poland, basically, to invest more. But they want to do it in a smart way,” says Andrzej Maciejewski, Babcock’s country director for Poland, who is based in Warsaw. “We’re addressing this ambition – that these great investments in defence will bring greater value for money and, in the longer run, these capabilities.” BAE Systems is partnering with the PGZ subsidiary Mesko, which makes ammunition and rockets, to build an artillery plant in Poland’s old southern industrial heartlands near Katowice. By 2028, Poland plans three new munition factories. During a visit to the Mesko facility in August, Tusk said figures for 2023 showed Poland was capable of producing only 5,000 rounds of 155mm ammunition – a Nato-standard artillery shells. “More is used in one day on the Russian-Ukrainian front,” he said. This year, Poland will have increased production to 30,000 rounds, with a goal of 200,000 a year in the next two years. This month, Luke Pollard, the UK minister for defence readiness, visited Czosnów for the opening of the MBDA facility. Pollard said it would help support jobs in both countries, including in Bristol, Stevenage and Bolton. Despite this, Britain is increasing defence investment at a slower pace . The government has committed to increase spending from 2.3% of GDP last year to 3%, but has not spelled out precisely how or when this will be achieved. View image in fullscreen Donald Tusk speaks to the media at airbase in Lask about the threat posed by Russian drones in Polish airspace. Photograph: Tomasz Stanczak/Agencja Wyborcza.pl/Reuters In Poland, there are signs its investment spree is beginning to pay off for local contractors. Maciej Klemm, the co-founder of Advanced Protection Systems (APS), which builds counter-drone systems in Gdynia, has increased its headcount from about 150 staff to 200 this year. Amid growing Russian drone incursions into Polish airspace, APS is playing a role in the Warsaw’s $4bn San programme to build an “anti-drone wall” to protect the country’s eastern flank. “We are spending a lot of money as a nation, and we are almost a poster child for it,” Klemm says. Splitting his time between Poland and the UK, where he still lives with his family after graduating from the University of Bristol in the 2000s, Klemm also sums up Poland’s recent economic history. “I was moving to Britain at the time there was a big wave of Poles coming over here. Now after Brexit, that wave partly receded and went the other way. Now, companies like ourselves and others are showing we have technical talent; we can build on this, and grow companies in Poland.” Explore more on these topics Poland Economics Arms trade Weapons technology European Union BAE Systems Europe features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Business Economics Diversity & equality in business Small business Retail

https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/31/zele.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has praised the US for its "strong decision" to approve the sale of 500 much-coveted Patriot missiles to Ukraine - but he has warned that delivery could take years.The US State Department announced on Friday that Washington had green-lit a package of Patriot PAC-3 interceptors worth $2.1 billion as Kyiv continues to defend against Russian missile and drone attacks."Five hundred PAC-3 interceptors is a substantial number, and very soon – this winter – they COULD make for a highly effective defence package," Zelenskyy wrote in a post on social media in response."However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS," he continued. "We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors."Earlier this week, Zelenskyy said Kyiv had been waiting for almost a month for US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth to sign off on a batch of missiles for both the Patriot and NASAMS systems.Kyiv has long called for more interceptors to help its forces fend off Russian attacks, and the rapidly approaching winter is pressing home that need. Russia has repeatedly sought to target Ukraine's power grid over wartime winter periods as Moscow has looked to break the country's resolve.Dwindling stocks of interceptors have already encouraged Russia to ramp up missile attacks in recent months, and there are fears this trend could lead to an especially brutal winter for Ukrainians."The United States, our European partners, and other partners around the world have sufficient stocks of PAC-3 interceptors in their warehouses," Zelenskyy said overnight. "Providing them to Ukraine right now – in the winter of 2026–2027 – and replenishing our partners’ arsenals LATER, in THE FOLLOWING YEARS, through this production already contracted and paid for by Ukraine and our partners would be the right approach."The Patriot missile platform is one of the world's most advanced air defence systems and can be used to defend against a variety of threats, including incoming aircraft and ballistic missiles.Ukraine receives the majority of its Patriots through NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative, which facilitates the purchase of military equipment and munitions from the US by allies and partners.As of June 2026, allies had committed to funding more than $6 billion of defence equipment for Ukraine through the scheme, per NATO.
